1) GFR is the best measure of renal function and that GFR is a better measure of AKI than changes in serum creatinine; 2) the measurement of GFR under steady state conditions remains the most reliable measure of GFR and that the measurement of GFB under non-stead state conditions remains a work in progress; 3) biomarkers of renal tubule injury have the potential to improve the diagnosis of AKI; 4) the performance of biomarkers of
the measurement of glomerular function and the detection of tubular injury biomarkers will provide complementary insights into the pathophysiological mechanisms of acute kidney injury (see Figure).
the combination of rapid measures of G FR and biomarkers of injury will yield substantive improvements in the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of AKI.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of novel biomarkers of kidney injury and their integration into a clinical decision support system to facilitate diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of acute kidney injury (www.kidneydecision.org).
the complementary roles of biomarkers of renal cellular damage and injury, and of rapid measurement of glomerular function in AKI.
the development of new biomarkers of renal function, the development of novel approaches for their detection, and their integration into the management of acute and chronic renal disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of biomarkers of renal tubular injury in conjunction with rapid measures of GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE will improve diagnosis, prognosis, and management of acute kidney injury (akireport.com).
the measurement of GFR under steady-state conditions remains the gold standard against which the performance of biomarkers of renal cellular damage should be assessed.

the measurement of GFR is essential for the diagnosis, staging, and prognosis of AKI and that biomarkers of injury are essential for the early detection of AKI and for the identification of the pathophysiological mechanisms of injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of biomarkers in combination with measures of GFR is likely to improve our ability to identify and manage patients with AKI.
the use of biomarkers in AKI is a work in progress.
the use of biomarkers to detect AKI is a work in progress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of GFR measurements to diagnose AKI is a flawed concept, because GFR is a dynamic parameter and the diagnosis is based on change from baseline GFR.
the combination of rapid GFR measurement and biomarker of injury is a more robust approach to the diagnosis and monitoring of AKI.
the measurement of GFR and biomarkers of renal cellular damage are complementary approaches to the early detection and treatment of AKI.
